utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon. You may proceed to call the case, Madam Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours. And may I say what a pleasure it is to be back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I share that feeling, Ms. Korner, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am attorney Milan Trbojevic. Lead counsel Mr. John Ackerman and, assisted by Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you both. So any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, as I'm back here, Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, it's very short, and it's simply this: We are amazingly enough reaching towards the end of the Sanski Most evidence, although there's a major witness to come tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you expect that witness to come tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on whether Ms. Sutherland can beat Ms. Richterova's record of calling a witness in chief. We probably think it will be tomorrow morning -- tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just this: As Your Honour knows, we obtained from Sanski Most the original of the, if I can put it that way, the Rasula diary, together with a number of examples of documents which we would say unquestionably written by him, court records and the like. I understand the Defence inspected it, and at the moment the Defence for General Talic -- I'm not clear what the position of the Defence for Mr. Brdjanin is -- is that this diary is not authentic. But unfortunately that doesn't help very much. We need to know a little bit more about what the basis is. In other words, is it suggested that it's not his handwriting? Because if so, we'll send it for handwriting comparison. Is it suggested that although written all in the handwriting which appears to be Rasula's, something else has happened? Your Honour, we need to know in order to be able to deal with it what the basis for the suggestion is. We'd like to be able to start the process before the summer break. So Your Honour, that's what I'm raising at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Zecevic or Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we contest Rasula's diary on several grounds. One is the contents of that diary. First, there are words in Latin script. Then the name of Rasula has been incorrectly written. That is, his first name. Also, this same witness, BT17, saw that he saw the journal in 1997 and there were no torn pages. We saw the diary which was shown to us -- which was shown to us by Ms. Korner, and at the beginning and at the end there are several torn pages. Also Witness 7.12 said that Rasula signed all his personal notes using also his father's name. In this diary, there isn't a single signature by Rasula mentioning the name of his father. On all these grounds we have every reason to challenge the authenticity of this diary, and we believe it is not Rasula's diary. We don't know who wrote it, but in any event we challenge its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that provide you with enough information?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if I understand correctly -- leaving aside torn pages and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- The rest, the only thing that we can do about it is if -- if I understand this correctly, is that it's not written by Rasula, so therefore we will have to do some handwriting comparisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one issue that came up or one aspect that came up last week when one of the witnesses- I don't remember whether it was BT17 or another one- was refer -- referred to a particular page in which there is indeed Latin -- or words written in Latin script, and it would appear on the face of it prima fascia that the name of Nedeljko is indeed written with an extra "J." That is, one instance that came up last -- last week. The other issue was the -- whether there were torn pages or not. I will not comment on that because the witness was categorically not at the same time. But that's about it. The rest was known already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, so you can take it up from there and work on it during summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I think what's more -- well, we will wait until the evidence has been completed of BT21, because I think he may be able to give Your Honours some assistance on this diary. But after that we'll take the course that we think proper. Thank you very much. Your Honour, then Ms. Sutherland is going to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. So this witness is not a protected witness, if I remember well. There's nothing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct? So we might as well -- usher, please bring the witness in. Ms. Korner, 7.119, we agreed that that witness will be brought forward at a later stage. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember who 7.119 is, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the one who had been --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just got a job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He's coming at a later stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Although we make take the decision, depending on time scales, not to call him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- 7.51, may he -- that will be in September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be in September, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that leaves us with this one, 7.62 and BT21, and that would close the chapter for the time being. Mr. Ackerman, aren't you contesting Rasula's diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would just adopt what Ms. Fauveau told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The gentleman who is standing next to you is going to hand you a piece of paper on which there is the text of a solemn declaration which you must make to us to tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It is the equivalent of an oath, and it is necessary for you to make before you start giving evidence. So please take that piece of paper in your hand and read out that statement aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. And that is your solemn undertaking to us, to this Court, that you will tell us the whole truth in the course of your examination here. You may sit down. And I will explain very briefly what's going to happen. The three of us you see here, we are the three Judges composing this Trial Chamber, and we are charged with deciding this case when it comes to that stage. You are here to give evidence, and you know that, because you obviously have been briefed. You will be asked a series of questions, first by one of the officers of the Prosecution, and after that you will be asked questions on cross-examination by the two Defence teams. Now, the members of the Prosecution team are to your right, and the Defence teams are to your left. In the front row there is the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin. In the back there is the Defence team for General Talic. It is important that you keep in mind that in answering the questions you try to answer the whole question and nothing but the question. Please don't go into details that are not asked from you, because otherwise you will stay here for days and days and days. You will not like it and we will not like it. So for your own benefit, when you are asked a question, try to answer that question and nothing else. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Sakib Muhic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 11th of April, 1939 in the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you the son of Fehim?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you practice a religion?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were married in 1964 and have two sons aged 33 and 25 years?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because I'm sure there must have been a mix-up in the interpretation here, because when he was asked for his ethnicity he answered a Muslim when he was asked for his religion, he answered a Bosnian. And when he was asked whether he practices a religion -- practices a religion, he said no. Are you a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, for me it's all the same thing, and that's why I said what I said. A Bosniak, yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of Islamic faith -- of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, I'll just repeat my last question. You married in 1964 and have two sons aged 33 and 25 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were born, until 1989, excluding 12 year that is you resided in Zagreb, have you lived in the part of Sanski Most town called Mahala?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Mahala, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a number of odd jobs. And in 1989 you opened a restaurant called Ribar, about 300 metres from the centre of town, which you ran until May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement to persons from the Office of the Prosecutor in April 2002?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That statement was read back to you by an interpreter, and you then signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the two women from the Tribunal visited you in July 2001 and that you signed a declaration at that time that the contents of your statement were true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I believed and I read it out - not everything - but that is more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague, were you asked to review your statement again?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed it and I read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon reviewing your statement, you wished to make a number of changes.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, I want to ask you some questions now in relation to events that occurred in the Sanski Most municipality in 1992. Were you ever taken to the cells directly behind the Sanski Most SUP building?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took me there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They took me. They came to my home. They took me to the cell over there behind the MUP building without going into the office. They handed me over immediately to others. They kept me there. They beat me up there. One day -- the second day, the third day, and then on the fourth day some men came - not many - and told me that my car had been used for transporting weapons. I showed them the car. It hadn't been registered for three months. I had a Mercedes 200. Then they went over there to the road, and they got as far as the road and said, "Look what kind of neighbours you had. They reported on you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Sutherland. Be patient.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The sound from the interpretation room is coming very, very faint. It's not a question of volume here, because the volume is as it was before. But I can barely hear what you're saying, although, of course, I can read the transcript. So please, if you could speak directly into the -- into the microphone, I would appreciate that. Yes. Sorry for interrupting you, sir. If you haven't finished, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three, Your Honour. Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I can hear you well now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you please speak a little slower for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You had said, Mr. Muhic, "I had a Mercedes 200. Then they went over there to the road and they got as far as the road and said 'look what kind of neighbours you have'. " They reported on you." That's when I stopped you. So you can continue from there then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, who are you referring to when you say "they" came to your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Vinko, a waiter with a weapon on the ready. Then Krunic, a former policeman, a policeman before the war; and some others. There were about ten of them; among them, some I didn't know. These two I mentioned, I know very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you just referred to as Krunic, how long had you known him for?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I had known him for a long time, quite a long time. He was a policeman for years and years. They also had a restaurant in the centre of town, "Three Brothers" the restaurant was called, "Three brothers."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit P668.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, while we're waiting for that exhibit, did you ever possess a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No, never. Not since I was born, nor did I have any interest in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the month that you were taken to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: It was just before Manjaca, about 15 days before, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you look at number 42 on the list that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Forty-two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if the English translation can be placed on the ELMO machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could do that, because this was not one of the documents that was indicated to us. We have 666 and 667 but not 668.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your name that appeared under number 42 on that list?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Forty-two? Shall I look through the pages? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Just 42. Under 42. There is a name Sakib Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says Osmanovic. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have a different document. P668 has the accused -- sorry, has the witness's name at number 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. 668. I saw 668 at the bottom of the page when it was being put on the ELMO. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The exhibit that Ms. Gustin has just hand me, Exhibit P668, has his name on the English translation but not on the B/C/S document. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What seems to happen -- I mean, I have 667, which at number 42 shows the same name, but there is no corresponding charge or accusation against any of those names contained in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the handwritten page which will now be placed in front of you, Mr. Muhic, can you look at number 42 on that page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that has the ERN 00493585.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you read what is alongside your name on that document.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I still haven't found my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Halfway down the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you help --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh. I've got it. Sakib Muhic. Here it's under number 42, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read what it says next to your name.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: "Smuggling of arms from Bosanska Krupa. Macanovic Mirjad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in arms smuggling from Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. I sold the man a part of Mercedes, to this one here, Macanovic, but his name is Mirsad and here it says Mirjad. Mirsad. I sold him a part of the Mercedes. I was never involved with weapons. If I had been, I would have been killed. Not just I; anyone else. So there you are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Muhic. I've finished with that document now.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you politically active?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No, I never was and I'm not active today either. I'm not involved with any parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understanding that these events happened ten years ago, do you have a good or not so good memory for events that happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I immediately said that I don't know nothing about dates, because I wasn't able to follow this either, because it was a matter of saving one's life. What do you mean dates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know whether you are of the opinion that you have a good or not so good memory of dates, as opposed to a good recollection about incidents which you eyewitnessed and which you will testify about today.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I know they went to Manjaca on the 6th of June, and someone else told me about that. When I gave my statement, I didn't know that. I'm not sure about dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will get to Manjaca in a little while. I want to turn now to another topic. What significant event happened in Sanski Most at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: At the end of May? At the end of May 1992 the radio of the so-called Serbian Republic asked us to go out of our homes, of our houses, and to go to the training ground where people would practice driving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do you recall what happened the day before you went to the training ground?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Before we went to the training ground?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night before you went to the training ground, do you recall what happened in Sanski Most town?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The night -- yes. Throughout the night Sanski Most -- that part of Sanski Most was shelled. From 9.05 up until the morning, when we started going out of our houses, leaving our houses, that's when the shelling stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what direction the shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The shells came from the direction of the right bank of the Sana, over in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they coming from the direction of Mahala, or were they directed towards Mahala?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They were directed to Mahala, over the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where were the shells coming from?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From Kljucka Street, from the bank. That bank belonged to the Kljucka Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the ethnicity of persons that lived in that settlement?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants in Kljucka Street, they were of mixed ethnicity. There were all sorts of ethnic -- there were all ethnic groups there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You started to tell us a moment that you went to the driving school. And you said that you heard it on the radio. Who made the announcement on the radio, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The announcement was made by the person working at the radio. His name is Miso Despot. We call him Miso. Perhaps his name a little different, but we knew him as Miso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was behind the announcement?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Behind the announcement? Well, he -- he composed this and he made the announce. There was no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he making the announcement on behalf of?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that, whether that's this person or that person. I didn't say that earlier on either, and I can't say that now. If I don't know, I don't know. It was probably, in my opinion, Vlado Vrkes and the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Vlado Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was the secretary and then he was the SDS president, of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Vlado? I knew his father very well, but I didn't know him that well. I know his father very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was -- on the radio, who was told to gather at the driving school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims. We were told to leave our houses, and if anyone didn't leave on time we knew what would happen. If anyone didn't come out, he would be done for, he'd be dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently hear about persons from the Muhici village who didn't comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That's not the village of Muhici. It's the Muhici Street which connects the centre and the bank. Well, let's say it goes up to bakery and a gynaecologist from Banja Luka was born there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Radislav Vukic. It goes right up to his house. The street goes right up to his house. Radislav Vukic's house, and he is a gynaecologist. He lives in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you -- what did you hear about the people that lived in the street called Muhici?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the training ground. And in the meantime, that same evening, eight people were killed in a shelter, and the oldest woman survived. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I asked you whether you had heard about the people that lived in the street called Muhici, whether you had heard anything about those people who did not comply with the order to go to the training ground. Are you able to tell the Court about that?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They were liquidated. They were killed if they didn't go to the training ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sutherland. This street called Muhici, was it previously known as Veljka -- Miljevica Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Miljevica. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Sutherland was asking you whether you knew on that street there were a number of persons who did not obey or follow the instructions that had been sent out on the radio. And if that is the case, what happened to them, that you know of, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, do you know a woman by the name of Vojnikovic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Vojnikovic, yes, she survived. An old woman. And in addition there were other people killed. There were two retarded persons who didn't understand orders. They were killed too in that Muhici Street. And then there are the eight people I have mentioned and there are others too, but I wasn't an eyewitness. So the figure is larger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How were those eight persons killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As there is a basement there and it shattered the window -- they shattered the window from the street. They threw in a few grenades. I don't know how many. And there were eight people who were killed. And Tanja Unic, a Croat, she was bearing a child. So we could say there were nine people who were killed and there was that old woman that survived in that basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, I want to concentrate on yourself now. Did you obey these instructions to go to the training ground?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Whoever complied with the order, nothing happened to that person. But those who were taken away on the other side -- we arrived at that school, the driving school. We were there for one hour. And on the other side there were about ten soldiers, on the other side of the asphalt. And about one hour later we were told to go to the football stadium, the Krkojevci football stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: And from there we --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to the Krkojevci football stadium, I want to ask you some questions about what happened on your way to the driving school.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers on your way to the driving school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: When we got to the driving school, the training ground, yes, we saw them. And on the other side I saw soldiers. Between 10 and 15 soldiers were there. On the other side, that's where they were. On the other side of the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Ruhdija Bajric?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of someone called Veli, Velic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Nail Selman?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Nail Selman, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man called Lola?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Lola, yes. Lola is his nickname. Veli -- Velic, that's his nickname. And Nail, well, that's the normal name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these men when you were walking to the driving school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Not to the driving school, but to the football stadium. Not the driving school. The football stadium which is 2 or 3 kilometres away from that training ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to the football stadium in a moment. After you arrived at the driving school, who was there when you arrived? How many people?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: It was full. There were columns of people standing there. And when everything was over, we set off in the direction of Krkojevci, to that playground Nail and these four men, Veli, and Lola, and Ruhdija, they passed by us. Their hands were tied and they were heading in the direction of the Krkojevci playground. So the road was about 6 metres away from us, and they were about 3 metres away from us. The entire column could see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were walking from the driving school to the Krkojevci football stadium approximately, and how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: We were all dressed in a normal way. Some people were wearing working clothes perhaps, but everyone was dressed normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in this column walking from the driving school to the Krkojevci football stadium?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to observe that immediately, so I -- noticed this when they put us in the hall in the evening. We were taken to the sports hall in the evening, so it was up to about 1.000 I'd say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will get to the sports hall in a moment. When you arrived at the Krkojevci football stadium --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there we sat down. We felt quite good. There was grass on the ground. It was a playground. So we felt quite good. Until Prastalo arrived. I know that they call him Kudra. He arrived in an APC Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and started maltreating us, cursing our balija mothers, and told us that it wouldn't be easy for us. Yes. And he provoked us in other ways too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall exactly what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, "We'll slaughter you -- they cursed our balija mothers, et cetera." He said terrible things. First of all he said, "God help you. Why are you silent, damn you," something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there military or police guarding you at the Krkojevci football stadium?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Up until dusk, a policeman or two -- and there were armed civilians around us. Towards dusk a large group of soldiers came from the direction of a forest. I saw that night was falling. They came to the stadium. I think there were 80 of them, at a distance or at intervals of 5 metres. Maybe they were crouching or kneeling. The women had started going and the children too, and we stayed up until about midnight, the men, and then they took us away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they took us," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally they were Serbs. There were buses there from Sana Trans, the transport company. They'd fill the buses up and off to the sports hall then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the men, women, and children taken to the sports hall who were at the Krkojevci football stadium?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That evening, yes, everyone. On the following day they separated the women and children and took them to the neighbouring villages. They didn't allow them to go home. They didn't allow them to return to their homes. By no means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the sports hall, was it guarded by military or police?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it guarded by the military or the police or both?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Police. There were other men there, but the police were there too. The torture in the hall wasn't that terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Normal police uniforms, the former police uniforms. And there were some colourful uniforms. I think they're military uniforms. Camouflage uniforms of some kind. And the police in blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: There were insignia, but mostly when -- on their caps there was a -- the Serbian flag, a flag of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally. Naturally they were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to leave the sports hall at any time?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't let us leave until they had decided who would go to Manjaca and who would remain. And then everyone was taken to Manjaca from there, after one month. And then I left on the 6th of June, and the others, I think they left on the 7th of July, one month later. My son and neighbours and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's a problem with the interpretation. On page 22, line 11 and 12. When the witness spoke about insignia, he said in fact that these flags were ribbons on the heads of the soldiers -- ribbons around their forehead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, you have heard what Madam Fauveau has just stated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. But if he had a high rank, he had a rank. Let's say the rank of captain, lieutenant, et cetera. I don't understand these matters very well because I served in the army a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy everyone? I don't think we went that far, but -- Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, you said that the following morning -- the following day that the women and children had to go to nearby villages. What were the names of these villages, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, the one that connects with the Sanski Most town -- the nearest village was Pobrijezje. That's where my wife was and my younger son, who at the time was 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of where these women and children went to after they were taken to these villages?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I found out, because immediately on the following day I was brought a roasted chicken and -- but she didn't find out about me. I wasn't there for three days. I -- she brought another one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife tell you or anyone else tell you what happened to the women and children who were taken to the village of Pobrijezje -- I'm sorry for my pronunciation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pobrijezje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: She told me that they had been received by the people from the village. Some people took them into their houses, two families or one family. That's how they divided the women and children. And people over 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that they were later taken to Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. I later heard that they tried to get through to Jajce. They got as far as Mrkonjic, Palanka, but they weren't able to get through so they were sent back. And only later did they head for Kladusa through Palanka and they arrived in Kladusa. They stayed there, and it was as if they were with the Serbs. They were with Fikret Abdic. He didn't give them any bread. He gave them nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the women, children, and elderly had left the sports hall, approximately how many men remained in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, in the first group about 143 of us left and went to Manjaca. That was the first group. Then after us, a month later, together with my son, and they counted them, and it was between seven and eight hundred people that arrived at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you please listen to my question. My question was: After the women, children, and elderly had left the sports hall, approximately how many men remained in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, we don't want to know anything about Manjaca for the time being. The question was referring to how many men remained in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you were taken --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I left, there were between 700 and 800 men left, and all of them came to Manjaca a month later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means between seven and eight hundred men, plus the 143, which you say left the sports hall earlier. Thank you. Were your particulars taken at any point --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: In my group, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your particulars taken at any point in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The sports hall, yes. They did take our particulars, for all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... particulars.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: For all of us. Spaso Cucak. He's still working in the council at the municipality. He took down all our data down to make sure that there would be no false accusations. So it's a good thing that we were all registered by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you were detained in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I was there for a brief period, briefly. In this large hall, maybe four or five days. And in the Hasan Kikic, like the gym -- but that's a hall too -- for two or three days. And that is when the 6th of June arrived with the trucks and came, and they moved us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to Hasan Kikic school and the 6th of June shortly. During the time that you were in the sports hall, did anyone come there and speak to the detainees? Anyone from the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. It was like this: Two Nivas came and called out some of the men. I was among them. And I was among the first to be interrogated by Branko Sobot, and I was the first to finish. And then he ordered somebody to put me below -- under the steps to wait.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just pause there. Mr. Muhic --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at me. Can you please listen to my question very carefully and answer the question that I am asking you. We will discuss when you were taken to the SUP and when you were interrogated by Mr. Sobot shortly. I'm now talking about the sports hall. I want to know whether during the time that you were detained there, whether anyone from the Serbian authorities came and spoke to the detainees there and, if so, who.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Oh, I understand now. It was Vlado Vrkes and the professor Nemanja. I don't know his surname. That's his first name, but I have no idea of his other name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did they speak to you for?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Maybe ten minutes. You climbed up a couple of steps, and they'd ask you this and that, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the nature of what they said?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They were saying that we would no longer have time to have coffee at Mindari [phoen]. I didn't know what Mindari were. And I asked what were Mindari. You won't be having a fine time and drinking coffee. I said, "Well, what's the point of life then?" Anyway, that's what they asked. Nothing much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your five-day detention, were you ever told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, your question why? I don't know why. Either because we are Muslims or because we did something wrong. Maybe that nation or that religion did something wrong in the past and this was some sort of revenge. I don't know. God knows. I'm no politician. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were at the sports hall, were you provided with food and water?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: We got everything, food from neighbours in the villages. My wife brought it while I was there and my son, normally. Maybe we were fed better than if we were at home in our own houses. Honestly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the authorities provide any food or water?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone mistreated at the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: While I was there, no. Afterwards I don't know. I left a month earlier to go to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that you were taken to the SUP from the sports hall. Do you recall the date, the approximate date that you were taken to the --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I said from the very first not to ask me about dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who you were taken to the SUP with?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: A taxi driver, Selman Himzo, Karlic Bedo, Bahtic -- anyway, it was Bahtic. I've forgotten his name now. And I know that we were taken to Hasan Kikic -- no, not Hasan Kikic. To Branko's, in a Niva. And there were several investigators. When the war started, there were 20 of them. But at that time there was just Branko Sobot, so I was through very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your interrogation with Sobot last?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say it was less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Not that much. When this one took me under the steps in the police building, then whoever felt like it would slap me or hit me, but not while I was at Sobot's. But I saw that this was no joke. He had bayonets, then a club in a glass case, and I realised what was it all about. But what could I do?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: And whoever came along, he would hit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left Mr. Sobot's office after an hour, where were you taken? Were you taken downstairs to under the stairwell?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, under the staircase. From Sobot's office down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to wait down there for approximately an hour?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I waited until they were through with everyone, and then we were taken back to Hasan Kikic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were downstairs under the stairwell for this approximately an hour's time, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I saw suddenly somebody saying, "Let's go. Let's go. Here comes the boss." And upstairs they were having a meeting and I was under the stairwell and they had to pass by. And then I didn't know who was in charge, but then they said, "Here's Basara. Here comes Basara." And then they ran upstairs. And then as someone passed, they would say, "Are you there too, brother?" And then the priest Milos came by and he said, "That serves you right, you balijas." He mistreated me most. And I was on good terms with his brother. And he liked to have a drink or two, and that's why he said that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you were taken then back to the Hasan Kikic school. You hadn't been there before, had you? You had been at the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Hasan Kikic school, who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I saw Dr. Sabanovic. I didn't even know that your eye could be 5 centimetres out of the socket. Then Ahmet Paun. I knew more or less all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it convenient for us to have a break at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Sutherland. We will have a break of 15 minutes or so, reconvening at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you try and relax as much as you possibly can. You may be a little nervous at testifying at the International Criminal Tribunal. Can you please listen to the question that I ask you and answer only that question. And if I need any additional information from you, I will ask you a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to make a correction, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned only one hall, the big one, the municipal one, that they didn't beat people there. But in Hasan Kikic, there was beating. In Hasan Kikic, they did beat us. And in the big hall while I was there they did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the Hasan Kikic school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I stayed there briefly, and I found others already there. So only three or four days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken from that school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From that school, a truck was brought first and a second was filled up next to the police station. There were two truck. One was a Deutz, the one I was in. The other was of a different make. I just know I was in the Deutz. And then we filled it up and went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many persons were on each truck approximately?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: In mine there must have been 70 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to sit down in the truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, hardly. We stood like sardines. But you always find a spot. So some people sat down, but some didn't. Until the end of the trip they couldn't sit down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the truck open or covered?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Afterwards they tied it all up, all around, and that is how we travelled. It took quite a long time to get to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see out of the covering at all?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No, you can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the trucks go directly from the Hasan Kikic school to Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. These two, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time in the -- what time of the day did you leave the Hasan Kikic school?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: We set off, I think, between 9.00 and 10.00. We got there towards evening, though the distance in kilometres is small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did the truck stop anywhere along the way?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Four or five times. Next to a store or a cafe, though we went mostly through the woods. So mostly shops. Then they would stop there, have a drink, whereas we were waiting, boiling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions in the trucks during this time.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The conditions were such that we almost could have said goodbye forever, almost. It was very hot that day. The tarpaulin was very tight. It's as if we were in a carriage for livestock. There was no water, nothing. We only just managed to arrive there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you arrived there towards evening. Were you allowed to get off the truck as soon as you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: We waited for a while, about half an hour, I think. And then there were some young people there. Who knows what could have happened. They started behaving as if we were tourists. I was among the older people. So then I also said, "You're not tourists. Calm down." But they were saying, "We can't stand it any more." And then they started hitting over the canvas. And then if anyone was leaning against the canvas with his nose, he would get a blow. And then when it was opened -- shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question. When you said "they," are you talking about the detainees in the bus -- in the truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: When I was saying that they should calm down, they wanted immediately to ask for water and various other things, and that's why I said that they were behaving as if they were tourists. And then they saw what was in store for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point were you ordered off the truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, after about half an hour. Get off. People were jumping out. Those they need were separated, six of them I think. I was among the last, and another waiter known as Sime, surname Bahtic, and then they separated six of them. And a superior -- his name was mentioned. I think it was Nemanja. I didn't know him very well or in the hall, but I remember his name being used. And he would say, "Come on Zenga." And when he said "Zenga," I peeped around and there were only the two of us left. And I stood -- I turned round looking. I didn't know who Zenga was. And then he pointed a finger, and he said, "You, you." And he jumped off and I was told to stop, and that's how it was. So beatings started straight away. Somebody called Apac, I think his name is Elvedin Hadziahmaetovic, they first fixed him. He was first among the six to die. Then Jasko Jelecevic. Only two of them had handcuffs. And then Pasic Marinko Faik, and after Faik was Neron, and then Biscevic Haris, and then this Sime Bahtic, that they called Zenga. With poles, with handles, broom handles and boots. I have saw them all go, but I was told to stop. And there was a small covered truck belonging to the Emis enterprise. As far as I could see, they were transporting food. And then they loaded all of them into this small truck. But then things slowed down. These passed away. And then Kajtez was last, and they said, "Kajtez, is it all over?" And then he said, "The balija is still showing signs of life." And then they loaded them all onto this small truck. And I was told to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, if you can just pause there. You have given a lot of information to the Court, and I want to take it in stages, the event that you witnessed -- that you have just told the Court about.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned six men, Bahtic; Jasmin Jelecevic; Medin Hadziahmetovic, called Hapac. You mentioned a man called Neron. What was Neron's family name, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Mehadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Haris Biscevic and --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Haris Biscevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Faik Pasic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Pasic, there must be six of them. Shall I now list them all in order?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. We have just listed the six men?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these men?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They were all of Bosnian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said two of them had handcuffs. Which two were these?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Hadziahmetovic and Jelecevic, who were closest to this small truck and they were the first to be loaded onto it. But they didn't have handcuffs -- the others -- the others didn't have handcuffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, what was Mr. Bahtic's occupation before the war?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was a waiter, in a socially owned catering establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelecevic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He would work with a small van transporting fruit and vegetables, and the same applies to Hadziahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Neron Mehadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Neron Mehadzic? He was a bus conductor in Sana Trans company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Haris Biscevic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Haris Biscevic? I think -- I'm a bit confused about him because another one got killed, his twin brother. As for Haris, I think they all followed in their father's and mother's footsteps, and I think they were all dentists. I know Buca who survived and he's a dentist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fajko Pasic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Fajko? He worked in construction. He was a construction worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they were taken off the truck, where were they taken -- who took them away from the truck?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The persons who -- the person who escorted the lorry got them off. And we thought that in each group, in each convoy, five of them would be designated, and they were there too, since Fajko wasn't designated, so he started beating them. So he started doing and spat at one of them and then they separated him. He was the third one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, you said that they were being beaten. Who were they being beaten by?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, a group of three or four men against one person. But no one was killed by a bullet from a -- with a weapon. And I know that someone who participated in this, this person who broke my arm, it's a neighbour of mine, Milan Camber, he participated in that and I know this person. And I know a person whose surname is Kajtez. And then I asked --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many persons were there in total surrounding these detainees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, about 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: In various ways. They were wearing this and that. But there weren't that many policemen -- I didn't see any policemen. But those who were wearing mixed clothes -- well, they were wearing all sorts of clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of them dressed in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this -- these mixed clothes were military uniforms. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, mixed or camouflage uniforms, yes. They had weapons, but they didn't kill anyone by using a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that they were beaten until they passed away. What kind of objects were they being beaten with?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, to be precise, there were these sort of sticks and cramp holders, things that you use in construction. And then parts of spades, those sorts of implements, those sort of items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You did mention wooden sticks a moment ago. How long did the beating last?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention sticks. You know -- I didn't mention any truncheons. You know what a truncheon is. These were the holders of spades. But yes, you could call it a sort of wooden stick. That's possible too. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland asked you how long did the beatings last.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It lasted about 20 minutes. About 20 minutes. Because no one had a watch. They'd taken our watches away in Sanski Most, and they took everything else away too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you observed these beatings?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Always at the back of the lorry. We were always there, in one spot. We didn't dare look anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were these six detainees and the soldiers -- sorry, the men beating the detainees. How far away were they from you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: There were three of them about 20 -- and then there was a circle and three of them were closer to us, not even 15 metres away. That was a semicircle. So they were a little closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how far away -- how far was the person furthest from you in feet or metres?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: 20 metres at the most from the lorry and from where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the person -- who was the detainee closest to you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: It was near the small lorry. Hapac was there and Jasko Jelecevic and Fajko Pasic. Because they were the first near the small lorry. They were sort of beside it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these men, besides Camber, who was doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This other person, I didn't know him. I don't know him. But they called him Kajtez. That was the surname they used -- they said, "Kajtez, is it finished? Have you finished?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Kajtez -- how did Kajtez respond?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He said, "Well, he's still showing signs of life. Damn his balija mother."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was Kajtez standing away from you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, he was where the victim was standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far in metres or feet was Kajtez from you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, 20 metres. It shouldn't be more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From the lorry. Yes, Kajtez and this victim I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe Kajtez for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Not very tall. He had a long beard, quite lively. He had lively movements. That's how I would describe him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of build did he have?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't a very big man. He was quite broad and average. He wasn't too fat. He wasn't fat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour hair did he have?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Black, black hair. But he had ribbon around here and all sorts of things up here. I know that his hair was black, not grey like mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how old did you think he was?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, as old as this neighbour of mine who knew him well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your neighbour that knew Kajtez well, and how old was he?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He went to school with him. So I asked him, "Who is this person called Kajtez?" He said, "Why?" I didn't answer. I said, "Who is he?" He said, "He went to school. We used to call him Kajtez Danilusko. And his nickname was Chetnik, even when we went to school together." I'd say about 40 years old, something like that. This neighbour of mine is 40 years old and they went to school together, Nedzad Mujagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention a moment ago that when these six men had been beaten to death, they were then put into one of the trucks. Did you see what happened after that to these six men?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: When I was told, "Go over there, balija, where your other people have gone," because that stable of mine is very close to the command, right up to the command gate. That's where we were, and that's what I was told. And after that, I was met by this neighbour of mine. He put my arms up like this against the lorry and made me spread my legs. He beat me as much as he wanted to and then he let me go. And then in the stable I came across another group. They were fighting those who had gone down already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will deal with that in a moment. Just getting back to when these eight men were beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit P781.2.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Six, six. Not eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I meant to say six.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. Don't put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Inspector Vujanic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Vujanic. He signed -- registered cars. When you went to have your car registered, he was the person who would sign the documents. That's why I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known him for prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, for as long as he was employed in the SUP, because I had a car and if nothing else, every year I had to go to the SUP and register the car. And once he had signed this, that would be it. You could drive your car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned already a policeman that you knew for a number of years called Mico Krunic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's a well-known person. Everyone knows him, just like this other person --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: -- Whom you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a man by the name of Vrucinic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Vrucinic, yes. He was also born in Kutilivac. That's not far from where I am. But I didn't know him that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see either of these three men when you were standing on the truck witnessing the six men being beaten to death?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I saw Vujanic around the truck. I saw someone called Njunja around the truck, the late Njunja. And all these main people, mostly when they were getting us into the truck, the tarpaulin was raised because they were loading the truck, and that's why I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw them at the SUP building before you went to Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Not in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I presume --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Outside. In front of the building by the truck, and they were regulating everything, deciding how to do everything and prepare for Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the truck arrived at Manjaca and you witnessed the beating of these six men, did you see either -- any of those three men that have just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been mentioned to you, that is, Vujanic, Mico Krunic, or Vrucinic, did you see either of those three men there that day?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see Njunja or the other men you have mentioned. Njunja escorted convoys too until he died. It was all one convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Njunja's first name and family name?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the town everyone calls people by using their nicknames. I knew everyone. I don't know their names. I wasn't that interested in it because people had nicknames. So I'm not interested now either. I didn't want to ask people about this. For me he was Njunja and he remained Njunja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we move back to Manjaca, when you were ordered to leave the truck. You said that you were beaten by a man called Camber.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What instrument was Camber beating you with?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That's what I said in Sanski Most too. He also used this implement, as in the case of the people who were killed. But he didn't kill me. But he beat me. He beat my arms. He beat me on the back. I had to position myself like this, with my arms against the lorry. He beat me up. They told him -- the others told him that "If you don't know how to beat, why are you beating him? Let him go." And he let me go, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any injuries to your fingers?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, on my body and on my fingers too, on the soles of my feet, all over my body. I was wounded all over my body. But when I went down to the stables, I thought I've got through. But when I got there -- well, it was -- you could imagine. And afterwards it was, "Ciao, balija, ciao." We covered ourselves with the blanket. "Well, dammit, we survived."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, just going back to when you were beaten before you went into Manjaca camp, do you recall what instrument you had been beaten with?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They used the spade handles mostly. Or if you know what a "glog" is. Well, it's something that had been prepared, something made of wood. And they used this to beat us with. It was something with thorns on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- was every finger on one of your hands broken by Camber?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally. Everyone in Sanski Most knows that I'd never been beaten, nothing had been broken up until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were two fingers of the other hand also broken when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please hold your hands up for the Court like this, Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That's all I can do. I can't move this one in this direction. I can't move the other one in that direction. There you have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the most you're able to straighten your fingers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't straighten them any more. I wish I could, but I can't use this hand to take -- to hold the wheel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that after you were beaten you came past the command post of Manjaca camp. Did you see any soldiers standing at the command post?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: At the command? All the other soldiers were down in the stable, and I went down there. If I'd been going a little more slowly, perhaps that all would have been finished. I got there when there was this beating takes place. I saw a man there. And he was all bloodied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: And I realised --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any soldiers standing at the front of the command post when you passed it to enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: To enter the camp? Well, this is how it was: They had all left the command. They'd gone down to the stable. That's where I came across a lot of soldiers, down there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers had left the command post. Were they there during the beating of these six men?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, they remained there. Those soldiers remained there. As far as I know, they didn't go down. I thought everything was over. And as there were soldiers down there and they were beating people -- well, at the end they said, "Ciao, balijas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of them were officers, these soldiers that remained at the command post?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see anything there. I couldn't look around. So as they beat people, well, they put some hay down on the ground and everyone had to lie down on the -- on their stomach. If someone hadn't been dealt with, he'd be dealt with. And that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the stable now, are you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, where I slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given that day or any other day any medical treatment for the injuries that you sustained to your fingers by the camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. But they suggested that I be released, that I be allowed to go home. And with this doctor, Sabanovic, there was also -- I don't know if he was a nurse. What's his name? But he was a Serb. And with Meho and Sabanovic, well, they thought they should release me, but I didn't go home. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date were you released from the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I think that was on the 14th of November. And the second group came, a young group, in a month's time, and my son was in that group. I joked. I said, "You'll follow me in one month's time exactly." And then he said, "How is that, father?" And then they escorted me to one gate and then to the command and he said, "How that, father?" And I said, "Well, your father knows everything." So it was exactly one month later they followed us to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, if we can just go back to the day that you arrived. Were there any other detainees in the Manjaca camp when your group arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
