utterances.text: We found only a few men from Grabska near Doboj. They were completing the construction of the camp. They came from a place near Doboj. I think there may have been 10 to 15 of them. They were tending the cattle when they finished the fence, and they milked the cattle. And I would give them a cigarette for a litre of milk, and that is how it went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you joined by any other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Croats came together with me. Then with me there were three Serbs in the camp. They broke the hand of one of them, and he wasn't given any kind of treatment. And Branko and I went to Karlovac together, and he was given a cast. Shall I go on talking? I can tell you what happened to him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. We will get to that in a moment. Did anybody -- did any other non-Serbs from any other municipalities join you in the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From the municipality -- let me think. There's the leather factory where -- further from Celinac a group of Croats came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone come from the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From Kljuc, they came from Stara Gradiska. They were taken there, to Stara Gradiska, to a prison there, a former prison. There were about 200 of them who came later. We arrived a little before them, because IFOR took over that place for their base. They looked terrible, nothing like human beings. They were all beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the group from Kljuc -- where were they detained?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They were detained in my stable, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and some loners from Doboj, from Derventa. They just happened to be in that same stable, like this Branko who was a Serb from Doboj. He had tried to escape the war. His father-in-law was a Croat. He hid in Slavonia. They captured him over there and they brought him to Manjaca. That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that they broke his arm and it was put in a cast.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Night had fallen, and two or three Muslims came very late. They were brought in late. And he was the fourth. And they asked his name -- their names, Smajo, for example, and when his turn came, he said, "Branko Stojkovic, what are you?" He said, "A Serb." And then this one said, "What kind of a Serb are you, you motherfucker?" And then they beat him and broke his arm. The nurse was there. He was a Serb, in Sabanovic's presence however. And I think they put a cast on his arm and he didn't take it off until we got to Karlovac. That was what happened to Branko. And there were another two Serbs, but I had no contact with them. He was in a different row. But I spoke to Branko a lot, and he told me everything about him. That's how I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness any other person being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: During the night there would be a call-out, and whoever was called out he'd know what to expect. It was terrible. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did the mistreatment occur?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Every night people were called out, at least five or six people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their condition when they returned?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They were broken up. It depends on whether you're lucky or not. Omer Filipovic was not lucky. Omer didn't return. Bender returned, Esad Bender, and he lived until 7.00 in the morning. He died in the stable, and the other one out there. And then we dug out a new hole that we used for garbage, and that is where we put Omer Filipovic, Senad, and an Osmancevic. I've forgotten his name now. We called him Ruski. These others somehow survived, but Omer succumbed immediately and this other one at 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. But in the transcript there's an error in line 18. The witness said that the people from Kljuc that came to Manjaca were all depressed. They didn't look like human beings. In the transcript it says that they were all beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have heard what Mr. Trbojevic has just remarked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trbojevic can interpret these things in two ways. I was saying that they came both depressed and beaten up. Of course, if they were depressed they were depressed because they were beaten. That's how it was, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that enough, Mr. Trbojevic? You may proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, did any international organisations visit Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: As far as the media are concerned and international organisations, let me tell you like this: Whoever wanted to come had to announce his arrival in Banja Luka. That is what they told us, the people from the Red Cross. And once they announced their arrival, then they would see what we were eating. Then they would slaughter three calves. And this meat would be put on the table --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when -- the first time the Red Cross visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know it was about a month and a half that I got plenty of bread. The important thing is that one has bread and water, and that's how you can gain weight. That's the important thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me try and understand, because I can't follow a hundred per cent here. Do you mean to say that after your arrival in Manjaca it was only a month and a half later that you started getting bread and water and started gaining weight again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Red Cross arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And at Manjaca we would get warm bread, coming from Sveta Klara in Zagreb, the large municipal bakery and when there was bread, everything was fine. And more -- later on kiwis and chocolate too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, I want to deal with the period before the Red Cross arrived. So you've just testified, I think, that the Red Cross arrived maybe a month, a month and a half after you arrived in the camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got warm bread and chocolates and kiwis. I want to deal with the period from when you were first detained in Manjaca on the 6th of June up until the time that the Red Cross first arrived. What sort of food were you given during that period of time on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: A loaf of bread would be cut into 45 to 50 pieces. It's like a matchbox, but thinner than a matchbox, but the size of a matchbox, but very thin. Sometimes there wouldn't be anything. But you still had to get up and pass through the kitchen and wait in line for everyone to pass by and then go back into the stable in line. That's all you could do. And -- shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What sort of -- yes, please continue. The question was: What sort of food were you given during the first month, month and a half in your stay in Manjaca? Today you've told us about the loaf of bread which was cut into 40 pieces -- 45 to 50 pieces. What else were you given by way of food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were given some lentils, something -- but I never touched it. There was some bacon too. I ate everything before and now, so that -- there are people who wouldn't eat bacon. "Give it to me," I said. So I did a bit better than they. I fared a bit better. And as for --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, was it before or after the Red Cross arrived that you were provided with bacon?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Before the Red Cross, of course. You'd get this piece -- tiny piece of bread and a piece of bacon. But I would have more bacon than bread, because they wouldn't give me bread. They would give me bacon. Shall I continue? But again, linked to the same subject. Shall I? Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, provided you keep it short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you about the media and the announcement. If you want -- if they wanted to show that they were feeding us well, they would slaughter three calves, three calves, so six halves. And then in the kitchen they would be moving around cooking until the delegation arrived. They were dealing with the meat. And as soon as the delegation leaves, they would take back those six halves and take it to the command and have a good feast. And this was welcome by the command. But they were telling them that that was what they were feeding us with, but none of us dared say anything. We didn't even see it. Only for as long as the delegation was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... more data from the witness on what kind of food he was receiving, what they were receiving. Please proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or next aspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, how much did you weigh before you were detained by the Serb authorities? How many kilogrammes did you weigh when you first went to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I'm ashamed to say. I'm ashamed to say. I had 104 kilos and I'm just over a metre high. But in that one month I dropped to -- not one month, a month and a half. Because the Red Cross came. There were the scales and everything. And my first weighing showed 55 kilos. So then the bread started coming. I never steal. We didn't steal from one another. But once the bread came, when I had -- had had enough, I was weighed again and I had 72 kilos. I said, "Is that possible?" And they said, "It is. Look." And it was only a month after the first weighing. I was doing better than a bull that they feed to gain weight. So I made up for the loss very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just eating bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. Ms. Sutherland, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, do you know who was in charge of Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means the person's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion -- I may be wrong regarding the rank. They called him Lieutenant Colonel Bogdan Popovic -- Bozidar. Bozidar Popovic. His deputy was a waiter from Banja Luka, a policeman known as Spaga. We called him Spaga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Popovic or Spaga ever present during mistreatment of detainees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, Spaga was present, and he actually did some beating. But Popovic less. He didn't expose himself much. I don't think he was interested in beating people or anything else. He himself didn't know what to do with himself. One could see that he didn't enjoy being camp commander. It was visible that he didn't enjoy it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Spaga with any lists of detainees?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was always carrying lists and calling people out and beating people as much as he liked. Each and every one of the detainees that were at Manjaca will tell you that. But the one who beat most as a policeman was Bulatovic. He was a driver in the brewery. He was really cruel. And another one called Zoki or Zaki, not the Zoki that used to play football. This one was good. There were two Zokas, Zorans. One was a good guy and the other was a bad guy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 667.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: What do I have to find here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, when you were spoken to before you gave evidence today by members of the Office of the Prosecutor, you reviewed this list, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- can you just have a look at that list once again.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at it. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many of these 105 people that are on the list were on the same truck as you were on the way to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, did I encircle this? I did or not? Capic? Stipe. I didn't make the circle. But it's all correct. Filipovic Omer -- yes. I got up to some 70 that were here in my truck. Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That document has -- the B/C/S version of that document hasn't been marked by you, but did you tell members of the Office of the Prosecutor -- did you tell them the number of each of the people that were on your truck? And it was approximately 60 to 70 people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that I didn't make these circles. But whoever made these circles made them for the same names that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go through several of these names with you. If I can say the number and the name, if you can give me the occupation of that person.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3, Husein Makic what was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was a forester, and now he's chief forester in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't need you to tell us the occupation now. I want you to tell us the occupation that they held in 1992. Number 4, Dr. Enes Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was always a physician, and a really good physician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 7, Mehmed Audic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Mehmed Audic, he's a farmer. If he's from Kutilivac, he's a farmer. What else could he be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the occupation of number 11, Enver Smailovic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was somebody working in an office. He has a law -- an economic degree, and he worked as an employee in the public utility company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 28, Ismet Veletanlic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Ismet Veletanlic, he was a carpenter and a glazier and he worked on the maintenance as a repair for the Hasan Kikic school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 29, Ivan Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Ivan Ivankovic, he comes from Kljevci, a farmer. He went to Batkovici. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 35, Fikret Malovcic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Fikret Malovcic, he used to sing, as his uncle did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sakib Seferovic?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Sakib Seferovic, he has a degree of some sort, a university degree. He's now working doing the job that Vujanic used to do issuing driving licences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, all of the people that I have just gone through with you, they were on your truck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of them to your knowledge involved in resisting in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, as far as the town itself is concerned, not a single bullet was fired, if you will believe me. Not a single bullet was fired. But someone would go over there, start shooting, and another one over there, and they'd say, "Look what the Green Berets are doing," as if we were naive and knew nothing. Not a single bullet was fired in town. I'm not saying that up there there was no resistance. In a village there was resistance, and they arrested five or six Serb officer over there and took them to Bihac, but they're still alive and well. The officers are alive, those who were taken to Bihac and beaten up, each other, each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, I'm finished with that document. If that can be taken away from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, you mentioned a village where there was resistance. Can you tell us the name of that village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Vrhpolje. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, finally I want to ask you what property you owned in 1992. Did you own land of approximately 100 square metres -- 1.000 square metres?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Just below my house, yes. I have no other land except that. It's what's called the house -- the land on which the house is built. I have no other land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own a three-storey house of approximately 300 square metres?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I still have it today. Because a Serb from Bihac lived there, and he looked after it and left it to me intact. I wanted to thank him. A machine of his was left behind. It's still there. It's used to make fishing equipment. His name was Zdravko Curguz, and I'd like to give it back to him. I'd be glad to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own a restaurant that seated approximately 50 people, and if so was it a successful business in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I was working well, until the very last evening. There was a birthday and business was still better when we were all together. And Serbs and Croats and everyone. That was the life. No one can say that it wasn't. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: And I had a tent too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: With some ten tables. So times four, so you can work it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also -- the contents of your house. You said that you've received your house back. Have you received the contents of your house, all the furniture and personal effects that you had in the house in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I didn't find anything. There's an old sofa -- I don't think that this Zdravko could have slept on it. It will do until I get some money. That will come too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, did you also own industrial refrigerators; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I had made by Ledo. I had a brother-in-law in Banja Luka. He was a boss of drivers. And he would always come. And this driver, he's now in America. His name is Majo Dzigumovic, and it was linked to Zagreb, to Ledo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Sutherland. One moment, Ms. Sutherland. I don't know whether the question that Ms. Sutherland put to you arrived, as it was -- as it was -- as it was described to us here. But Ms. Sutherland asked you whether you also owned industrial refrigerators.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Those are smaller ones. Yes, industrial freezers. Of course, I had a small one to keep my meat in, my own food in, yes. I had the small refrigerators. I don't have them now. I brought a refrigerator from Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I was told that I didn't have any left over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, if you can just answer yes if that's correct, the list of things I'm going to read to you that you owned in 1992. We've said your land, your house, the restaurant, the industrial refrigerators, two poker machines, a pool table, and a football machine. You also owned a shop that you had in summer in front of the house selling carpets, and within that shop in 1992 there were approximately 50 or so carpets.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. A billiard table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also owned a Mercedes 200 motor vehicle and a small car.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in those days I had a shop, and I had stocks which I hadn't sold, and then I opened a restaurant called Ribar. So I had those 50 carpets stored. They were not on sale any more. I no longer had a shop. So that is right, what you're saying. I can't say that I isn't. As for looting, I didn't see it but I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- besides the land and the house, do you have any of the above property left?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing remained. I only found rubbish. For ten days I rummaged through it, and nothing remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since the injury that you received in Manjaca to your fingers, have you been able to work?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, if I were able to -- I like to keep busy. I'd do what I can now if I was given the opportunity, but I don't have any income. I've got those four walls. But it would be better for me to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Muhic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Who's going to go first? Now, Mr. Muhic, listen to me. You are now going to be asked a series of questions by Mr. Trbojevic, who is the co-counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. May I point out to you that Mr. Trbojevic is carrying out a duty here. He has an obligation to defend his client and, therefore, to put questions to you. So please, I'm telling you this because I want you to answer all the questions that he puts to you unless I tell you not to. But if you don't hear from me, please answer the questions that Mr. Trbojevic puts to you. And the same would apply later on when you are cross-examined by the other team. Mr. Trbojevic, you have more or less 12 minutes before we break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know. I've got no idea about this. These statements of mine, what do they have to do with Brdjanin? I don't know the man. So I'm just asking you this question. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about Mr. Brdjanin. Don't -- you don't have to worry about it. For --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I'm worried about myself. I never said anything about Brdjanin and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have to worry, because no one is attributing to you having said anything about or against Brdjanin. So don't worry about it. But still Mr. Brdjanin's lawyer has a right to cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say anything about Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Trbojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I agree that what you said has nothing to do with Mr. Brdjanin. In your statement which you gave initially, you said that officials from the Party of Democratic Action would come to your restaurant.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, look, just as you don't know about certain things, I don't know who these people were. All of a sudden Njunja didn't turn up. He wasn't there for a few days. He was the president or the commander of the SOS. This person wasn't there. That person wasn't there. There were no Serbs. Only, Marko Macura [phoen] remained. I don't know whether they were there to spy on me. He know that is better than I do. I had my business. I'd have something to drink in the evening, and that's what I was interested in. Nothing else interested me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it could be that my memory is failing me, but I don't recall having heard the witness mention anything about the persons party -- members, officials of the Party of Democratic Action visiting his restaurant. There is something in the statement and not precisely on the Party of Democratic Action. It's more or less on certain particular individuals. But I don't recall him mentioning anything during the -- the direct. Did he mention anything, Ms. Korner or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, or Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions about this subject after this answer, your.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were in two halls, in two sports halls?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. In one of them they beat us, but I wasn't beaten. And in the other big one we weren't beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many days you spent in each hall.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there for a short time. Sabanovic, the doctor and so on, they were beaten and they were there for a long time. They were in the small one. I was in Hasan Kikic. And in the big one my son was there. When he came after a month's time he said, "Did anything happen to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you?" I said, "Nothing." I would rather that I had been beaten than the child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that was two or three days in each --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Please. I am going to call you both to order. First you, Mr. Trbojevic. You are committing the mistake that you had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Muhic. Please listen to me. Look at me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got an answer. I've got an answer for Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please look at me. From now onwards, before you start answering the question that Mr. Trbojevic puts to you I want you to look at me and I will tell you, "Yes, go ahead." Before I tell you, "Yes, go ahead," please don't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Trbojevic, please don't jump into the next question the moment -- or even before the witness has answered your question. So your question, Mr. Trbojevic. I'm sorry I have to bring it down to this level, but there is no other way we can deal with it. Mr. Trbojevic, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, can you tell us, the six men you saw in Manjaca, were all of them or some of them with you in the lorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said, Mr. Muhic. Look at me before you start answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fajko Pasic. Only Fajko Pasic wasn't in the same lorry -- in that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you know, from which parts of Sanski Most were these six people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I said wait until I give you the go-ahead. Now you have the go-ahead. Please answer the question. Well, Trbojevic, leave that alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they from a particular area such as Mahala, or were they from various parts of town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My neighbours. They were all my neighbours. Some of them were waiters some conductors. They were all neighbours. And when I gave my testimony I said, "These people who understand me --" that's what I said. You don't understand me. You're a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the centre. From the central part of the town. That's right. People I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- one moment. Mr. Trbojevic, could you repeat your question. The witness need not answer it. But we had no translation, at least in the transcript. And neither in the interpretation. I couldn't hear anything. What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness whether I was right, if I said that these six people, whose death he saw in front of Manjaca, I asked whether they were all more or less from the centre of the town of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And he answered from the centre. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Next question, Mr. Trbojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic or Madam Fauveau. I don't know who is going to conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And shall we break now and you start immediately after? What do you prefer? You still have another five minutes. That's all. But I -- probably it would be more convenient to break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be better if I started after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Okay. So that's -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to say this: I have to be elsewhere at 6.00. But Mr. Cayley will be replacing me for the remaining hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, for keeping me -- the Chamber informed of that. Thank you. We'll reconvene in -- at half past -- half past 5.00. One moment. Madam Fauveau, do you think you will finish in one hour?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think I will finish in an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Muhic, you are now going to be cross-examined by another lawyer, this time one of the Defence counsel for General Talic. Madam Fauveau, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said just a minute ago that you had a restaurant in Sanski Most and that at the beginning the Serbs also went to that restaurant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, everyone. Gypsies, all peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at a certain point in time no one else went there apart from Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, a lawyer, he went there right up and to the end. Now a chief of the police of the Serbian -- Sanski Most, Macura Bandzi. I don't know what happened to him. There were no documents. Everyone would go to my restaurant. But that stopped after a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mention the names of some Muslims who went to your restaurant.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I could. But if it suits you, yes, provide you with some names. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Adil Draganovic went to your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. He was never a guest of mine. The president of the court, he didn't turn up. Why? I don't know why Adil Draganovic didn't go there. He never came to have a drink, but he likes to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor show the witness his written statement of April 2000 in the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness's answered when we're talking about Draganovic, it wasn't correct interpreted and entered into the transcript. The witness explained that if Judge Draganovic liked to have a drink and liked to have a drink for free. That's a provincial expression which means that someone wants to drink without paying. But he said that he didn't go to his establishment. And that's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know for sure that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you heard what Mr. Trbojevic has just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I agree with Trbojevic and this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Madam Fauveau, please put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you have a look -- it's on the second page in the Serbo-Croat version. It's the last sentence. And it continues on page 3. And in the English version it's on page 2 and it's in the last paragraph. You said: [In English] "Among the Muslim who is came to my restaurant, many were SDA officials and police officers. I guess they felt safe on any premises. The SDA officials included Adil Draganovic, judge of the local court; Mirzet Karabeg, a lawyer working for a company; Rifet Bahtic, a psychologist at the local hospital; and many others."

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as the SDA is concerned -- if it was some party -- some other party, that would be possible. But the SDA, no, by no means. But that was an establishment where all peoples went, all ethnic groups. But when you say the SDA, that can't get by. So please ask me no more questions about that. I can't accept the SDA, if they say the SDA. I'm not a member of any party, and I don't remember saying that. If you know what a man of the world is -- well, it doesn't matter -- for such a person, it doesn't matter what the name of such a person is, what he is, who he is. Nothing bothers me. If he comes back, he can be chased by someone else if he's guilty of something. I have nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this person didn't go to your restaurant. But is it true that this person was a member of the SDA -- or the persons whose names I have read out to you, is it true that they are members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They could come. But how am I to know who they are? They can go to the restaurants. So don't ask me who is from which party, because I wasn't interested in that. And everyone had the right to go there, as I previously said. Because I made no distinctions among them. They did that themselves, but not me at my cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day of the attack in Sanski Most, you said that the shelling came from Kljucka Street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From the right side of the -- from the right bank. And the Kljucka Ulica is at the rear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this part of the town, the population was mixed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that street and in that part on the right bank it was mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on you heard about a tragic event in which eight people died as a result of a grenade that had been thrown into a house. Did you personally witness this attack which was carried out against this house?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see that. On the following day this was especially not possible. I was already on -- at the training ground. I had left my house, and I had set off. I know that there were some sort of a board and there were some sort of names there. It was a sort of commemorative plaque. I didn't go to see that either. I know that they were buried in our cemetery and they were exhumed from a grave, but I didn't go to see that, to see them in such a condition at least. And as I didn't see them, I can't describe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that it is the neighbour of these people who threw the grenade into the house?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I heard. Some Sergije Dobrijevic. I know him. He was a civilian up until the last day. I don't know if he donned a police uniform. I have no idea. But that's what I heard. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was an announcement on the radio according to which all the non-Serbs had to gather in front of the driving school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In front of this driving school, were there any policemen, any soldiers, or people of Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Not in front but behind, on the Kljuc-Prijedor Street, about 10 to 15 people -- 10 to 15 men, as I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these Serbs dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: In various ways. They had mixed clothes. They had a shirt here and they had cockades and some ribbons around their heads. Nothing else. That's what they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went to a sports hall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: From the training ground? No. The Krkojevci football stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. And at this football stadium there were Serbs there too, were there not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: They were to come -- they came at dusk from the forest. As night fell, then they took the women away. The men remained, and they lined up around the playground at intervals of 5 metres. There were quite a lot of them. And then we became afraid. There was Kudra, who was in the APC, and he said, "God help us," and some people answered, some others didn't. And he said, "Why are you remaining silent? Damn you, you balijas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people who came to the stadium, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a sort of olive colour, and some people had black clothes on. But it was mainly -- they were mainly clothes of an olive colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Prastalo, whom you have called Kudra, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I think that he was in civilian clothes. I saw him in the -- I only saw him in the transporter, because we weren't allowed to raise our heads. I had a look at him like this. The APC was about 20 metres from me. And he was standing alone on the APC, and he is the only person I saw there. He was wearing civilian clothes, a black T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went to the sports hall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. It took us a long time to get there -- to go there. It was midnight. That was in the beginning, in the morning, when he turned up in the APC. And on the APC it said, you had the words "Crni Djordje," "black Djordje."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true say that once you went to the sports hall someone called Spaso Cucak had a list of people who were in that hall?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Spaso Cucak in the middle of the hall. He put a table in the middle of the hall. I was lying down under the handball goal. I wasn't worried about anything. It was good for me, and that's where I was. And then my son said, "Father, it started with the letter M." I said, "You go ahead, son. I'm not very good at this. Write down both our names." And that's what he did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that Spaso Cucak, who was also wearing civilian clothes --

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he is in the council. He works now. And I see him quite often, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your detention in the sports hall, someone came and brought you food -- your wife came and brought you food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. She brought me a roast chicken on one day, and then she did the same another day. But I wasn't there. I was transferred to Hasan Kikic and no one wanted to tell her this. Yes. Because I gave Sobot a statement. He wanted to ask me about the cafe. I said, "Sobot, you know what my job is." So I'm not very interested in politics, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were detained in Sanski Most, would it be correct to say that your wife was in Pobrijezje?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was in Pobrijezje, and she asked those people of mine -- she asked those Serbs, "Where is Sakib? Where is my Sakib?" And Njunja said, "Sakib is a in safe place," and he told her that. At that time I was already in Manjaca, yes. So I can say that afterwards it was better for me in Manjaca than in the town during the period that the Red Cross took care of us. But initially, no, it was -- you'd die of starvation. I was told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enough. Enough. Next question, Madam Fauveau. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your wife came to bring you food in the sports hall, she was coming from Pobrijezje, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were interrogated by Sobot, a police officers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was that before. Then there were newcomers. During the war people became lawyers and prosecutors, and I knew what they used to be and now they are pretending to be something else. And this list --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you first, please. While you were waiting for other people to be interrogated by Sobot, you said that you heard somebody crying out that Basara was coming; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see this person that was allegedly Basara?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Only when he passed by me. That is when I saw him for the first time, and I saw that they were running upstairs and saying, "Here comes our boss." Yes. And then this priest Milos provoked me a little bit. And I was a great friend of his brother's. This one was a priest, and the brother liked to have a drink or two. And so the brother didn't like that very much. But I didn't care. This list was written by the person who had accused me of feeding the SDA. He wrote this list, I'm sure. Now you try and find out who wrote this list. This is not part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, you are not answering the question and nothing but the question. You are barely answering the question and a lot of other thing that is have got nothing to do with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Fauveau, your next question. And let's hope he will answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did see Basara. Did you see the clothes he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: A camouflage suit, and there was a rank here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known Basara from before?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I had not, but I had heard of him. I hadn't seen him before until that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person who was saying that Basara was coming, did he mention the name Basara or did he just say that their boss was coming?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said "boss" and "chief" and all kinds of names they used to refer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question was a very simple one, Mr. Muhic, whether his name -- that is, whether the word "Basara" was mentioned or not. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basara, yes. Yes. I don't know any other -- everyone calls him Basara, his subordinates and this one and that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So on that occasion you heard that name being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because on the ground floor it was crowded, there were civilians and policemen that used to be policemen from before and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. -- Madam Fauveau, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were transported to Manjaca, you were transported in a truck. That was a civilian truck, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. It used to be owned by companies before, belonging to companies, yes. They were being used, just as they used the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of a certain Mr. Bahtic. Is it correct to say that this Bahtic used to fight with the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the surroundings of Livno. That is why they referred to him as Zenga. I learned that afterwards, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this Bahtic was fighting with the Croats against the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned an SOS unit and you said that Njunja was the commander of that unit. Did you know whether Kajtez too was a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. But close, but I'm not sure. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Camber was a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: These were city boys, so you can't know. But they engaged in blowing up Muslim businesses and that sort of thing, this SOS. They didn't destroy mine, so they apparently liked me as a caterer. What else can I say? That's how it was. But they destroyed many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Kajtez had a ribbon round his head. Did Camber have the same kind of ribbon round his head?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. He was mostly their driver. He would drive the convoys where necessary. He was a driver. He's a driver and mechanic by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed during that transport to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: He was wearing an olive-grey uniform, and he had two bandoliers, if you know what they are. Whether there was any ammunition in them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of Omer Filipovic. Did you see Omer Filipovic the night when he was called out together with Esad Bender?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Bender was regularly with us, but he was not. He was in the isolation cell for a month, outside the stable, near the kitchen. He was in that isolation cell. And then they apparently released him, and we had to make it possible to be 15 metres away from us so that no one could contact him. And we did so. No one could approach him. He got as far as the entrance of the stable, got hold of a railing used for cattle, and he was standing there, and then he was called back and he crawled back, and we didn't see him again. And then that hole -- another Osmancevic and Senad, Supuk and Bender. Bender died at 7.00 in the morning and Filipovic passed out immediately. And then we would dig out a hole for garbage. Once it was filled, we'd have to cover it up and then we would dig a new one. And that's how it went. And the same applied for a toilet. We'd dig a trench ten metres long, put two planks across it, fill it up, as soon as it was filled with earth, then we'd have to dig out a new one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day were you able to see Filipovic's body?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Only when they were loading him onto the car. He was put in a blanket and driven off. And then they added Esad Bender that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us around what time you saw those bodies put in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Before noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Was it very early in the morning or a little later on?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: About mid-morning. After breakfast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right to say that the first day you arrived at Manjaca you had blankets in the stables?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: When we arrived? Yes. One had blankets. You could have two. You could have both to cover yourself with. But it was summertime, so we didn't really need it. But when winter came, we had as many as we wanted. The Red Cross would give four or five blankets. They just asked you how many you wanted. We could have taken ten blankets when the Red Cross came. And when we arrived, there was just hay covered with blankets. We had the advantage that we had wheat hay, which is a little better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that after the Red Cross arrived in Manjaca, the conditions in Manjaca were more or less correct, acceptable?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Acceptable, yes. There was less beating, all of that. Then they checked us, those girls from the Red Cross. Every day someone would be there. It was easier to breathe. One felt more relaxed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the women -- that some women and children of Sanski Most left for Velika Kladusa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. In about 12 buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Velika Kladusa in those days was under the control of Fikret Abdic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's why he didn't give them any bread to eat, not even if they paid for it, to the refugees from Sanski Most. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the conditions in Velika Kladusa were no better than they were in Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Well, he would keep all the humanitarian aid in Kladusa for his people. As for those who were not his, especially people from Sanski Most, he wouldn't give them anything, even though they came in a convoy via Croatia, the refugees had no benefits. I had a 13-year-old son with Fikret Abdic, and he had to cut wood for the -- Fikret's men just to be able to eat. He is now 25 years old, my dear child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Fikret Abdic was a Muslim, was he not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: So what? They're always all kinds. You think that if he's a Muslim that he couldn't do anything like that? Is that what you think? Let's go and rest. We've had enough of this. Please. INTERPRETER: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when you returned to Sanski Most your house was intact but looted. Can you tell us when you returned to Sanski Most after the war.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Nothing. In 1996 -- again I don't know the date. Honestly I don't. I just don't know dates. In 1996. I cleaned it up a little bit. You know how it is. One likes one's own yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So actually, between your departure from Sanski Most and your return to Sanski Most, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had entered Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that army chased the Serbs from Sanski Most, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time you were detained in Manjaca and while you were a refugee, a Serb lived in your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zdravko Curguz from Bihac. Yes. I said his machine is still there. I'm doing my best to find him. I don't know where he is, in Derventa or something. I'd like to give it to him so that he can work with it. He looked after my house, but nothing is left in it. I admit he didn't take it with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have already told us all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But actually you don't know whether he took your things or whether it was the Bosnian army when he was chased out of the house.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. My things had gone when my wife came from Pobrijezje. She came once to get some underwear, to take it to the village in Pobrijezje, and she saw that already then the house was empty. It is known who did it. I mentioned it. But when these minor culprits are hold to account in Sanski Most, we'll come to that. And who knows whether they will ever be held accountable for looting and all those things, but they should. This man came from Banja Luka and did these things -- not from Banja Luka, a neighbour. He came to Krkojevci and said Milos Trpko's father came. I used to fish with him before the war. But I don't do that any more. But still I will never attack him, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right to say that you consider your neighbours in Sanski Most responsible for what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. No one came from the outside to beat me, from Prijedor or from anywhere else, but my neighbours. It's not just that I think so, but that's what it is. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just two matters, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Muhic, just on this one question that you were asked by Defence counsel that, you consider your neighbours responsible for the thing that is happened to you. What ethnicity are you speaking of, when you say your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: The Serb group, the SDS. Let me mention the name of the party too. The SDS party, which is of course a Serbian party. That's right, isn't it? The SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other question -- one other matter. Just to clear up the date of when your house was looted. You said that your wife came to visit you from the village of Pobrijezje. I can't pronounce that. I'm sorry. That was when you were detained in the sports hall in the beginning of June, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she told you when she visited you that your property had been broken into and all the property had been looted.

utterances.speaker: SAKIB MUHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no questions from the Bench, which means, Mr. Muhic, that your testimony has now come to an end and that you can go back to your hotel and rest before you go back to your country of residence. Before you leave this courtroom, may I on behalf of the Tribunal thank you for having come over here to give evidence. And let me assure you that between now and your return to your country of residence you will be attended to as you may require. If you have any problems or any difficulties, please do contact the authorities of this Tribunal and they will look into the matters. I thank you. The usher will now escort you out of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you too. And I'm glad that no one is angry with me and about what I said. I'm glad about that. Thank you all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else before we wrap up and go to rest as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the understanding is that we will resume tomorrow at 2.15 with BT21, that being a closed session, if I remember well. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could get some kind of an indication as to how long the direct examination of this witness is going to require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who's going to conduct the direct? Is it you, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President. I have to say to Mr. Ackerman that at the moment, no, I've got no idea how long the direct examination is going to be. It's going to be longer than a few days. It depends how quickly I move through the documents. It depends on how long the answers are. When I do have a firm idea of where I am, I can let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The obvious -- the question was obviously being put because of Monday. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is being put because of Monday. I intend to be -- to do the cross-examination of this witness, but because of this sort of last-minute change in the schedule I can't be here Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't realise you -- a week on Monday we say. Not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Because the week 15th to 18th we will be sitting in the morning and not in the afternoon. And so happens -- I mean, there was an understanding between us that we would see where we stand or where we'll likely be Monday because if that would be the day when the cross-examination is supposed to start, then obviously we were going to have a problem, both with Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Ackerman, both arriving on -- sometime during the morning on Monday and not being able to be present here to conduct the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I take it -- one moment. As I take it, we have this witness starting tomorrow, Tuesday, and then we have Wednesday, and that's it for this week because Thursday and Friday we have the plenary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We don't have Wednesday either. You just have one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we don't have Wednesday either. Exactly. We don't have Wednesday either. Wednesday we have the other issue. So we only have tomorrow, which means that this witness will continue on -- definitely. Because if I read you well, you are talking of days, not -- not hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll take it up tomorrow towards the end, Mr. Ackerman. Rest assured that I will try to accommodate you all as much as we can. You know, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears there's no problem if the witness is on direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. The witness is -- will be definitely on direct on Monday --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can have the transcript on Monday and be right back with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And if necessary, even if it is a closed sitting, I can procure tapes or whatever if -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you Mr. Cayley. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman and of course everyone else. Have a nice evening. We will meet again, please God, tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
